title: Helmet First
bigQuestion: What do skaters do before they roll, so a fall is a small one?

story.title: The Strap Check Line
story.kicker: No one rolls yet. First, every helmet gets checked by a friend.
paragraphs: It is skate day in the gym. Six boards rest on the floor. Nobody stands on them yet. Coach Rivera claps two times. The class lines up in pairs. Each child holds a helmet.
"Helmets on," says Coach. Maya puts hers on. It sits low on her forehead. Her partner, Jon, holds up two fingers. They fit between her eyebrows and the helmet. "Good," says Jon.
Next, Jon checks her strap. It is buckled. He slides one finger under it. The strap is snug, not tight. Then Maya checks Jon. His buckle hangs open. He clicks it shut.
Then come the pads. Knee pads. Elbow pads. Wrist guards. Everyone wears flat sneakers. Coach looks down the line. "Now we are ready to learn," she says.
story.think: Why do you think the class checks helmets before anyone stands on a board?

lessons.title: A Helmet Guards Your Head
lessons.mainIdea: A helmet has soft foam inside that keeps a bump from hurting your head.
reading: Your head holds your brain. Your brain helps you think, see and move. A fall can bump your head. A *helmet* is a hard hat that guards it.
Look inside a helmet. You see thick foam. The outside is a hard shell. If you fall, the shell spreads out the bump. The foam squishes. It soaks up the hit, so your head does not get it all.
Skaters wear a helmet every time they ride. Put it on before you step on the board. A helmet that took a hard hit may be worn out. Ask a grown-up to check it.

words.d: a hard hat with soft foam inside that guards your head
soft, squishy stuff inside a helmet that soaks up a bump

look.title: Egg in a Cup
look.text: Look at two eggs. One egg sits in a plain cup. One egg sits in a cup full of foam. Both cups tip over onto the rug. The foam hugs the second egg. It soaks up the bump.
look.prompt: Which egg is like your head inside a helmet? Why?

check.q: What does the foam inside a helmet do?
check.why: The foam squishes when you fall. It soaks up the hit so your head does not get it all.

check.q: When should a skater wear a helmet?
check.why: Skaters wear a helmet every time they ride, even on flat ground.

check.q: What should you do if your helmet took a hard hit?
choices: Keep using it and say nothing
Ask a grown-up to check it
check.why: A helmet that took a hard hit may be worn out. A grown-up can check it.

lessons.title: Snug and Buckled
lessons.mainIdea: A helmet works best when it sits low, fits snug and is buckled.
reading: A helmet must fit. It should be *snug*. Snug means close, but not squeezing. Shake your head. A snug helmet does not wobble or slide.
First, set it low on your forehead. About two fingers fit between your eyebrows and the helmet. Next, the side straps make a V under each ear. Then click the *buckle* under your chin.
Now open your mouth wide. You should feel the helmet pull down a bit. About one finger should fit under the chin strap. A helmet tipped back or left open cannot do its job.

words.d: close and steady, but not squeezing
the clip under your chin that holds the helmet strap shut

look.title: The Two-Finger Check
look.text: Look in a mirror. Put on your helmet. Lay two fingers flat above your eyebrows. They touch the helmet edge. Now find the straps by your ears. They make a V. Click the buckle. Slide one finger under the strap.
look.prompt: Try the two-finger check with a partner. Does the helmet sit low enough?

check.q: Where should a helmet sit?
choices: Tipped back on top of your head
check.why: A helmet sits low on the forehead, about two fingers above the eyebrows.

check.q: What does snug mean?
check.why: Snug means close and steady but not squeezing. A snug helmet does not slide.

check.q: What do you do right after the side straps make a V?
check.why: First the helmet sits low. Next the straps make a V. Then you click the buckle.

lessons.title: Pads and Wrist Guards
lessons.mainIdea: Knee pads, elbow pads and wrist guards cover the parts that hit the ground first.
reading: When people fall, knees, elbows and hands often touch down first. Pads cover those spots. A *knee pad* has a hard cap on the front. It lets your knee slide instead of scrape.
Elbow pads work the same way. A *wrist guard* has a stiff piece along the palm. Wrists get hurt a lot in skating. Wrist guards help keep them safe.
Pads must fit too. Pull each strap so the pad stays put. A pad that slides down cannot cover your knee. Wear all your pads while you learn.

words.d: a cover with a hard cap that guards your knee
a glove-like brace with a stiff piece that guards your wrist

look.title: Count the Gear
look.cite: A full set of learning gear, counted piece by piece
look.prompt: How many pieces of gear do you put on in all?

check.q: Which body parts often touch the ground first in a fall?
check.why: Knees, elbows and hands often touch down first. Pads cover those spots.

check.q: What does the hard cap on a knee pad let you do?
check.why: The hard cap lets your knee slide on the ground instead of scraping.

check.q: Why do skaters wear wrist guards?
choices: Wrists get hurt a lot in skating
check.why: Wrist injuries are common in skating. Wrist guards help keep wrists safe.

lessons.title: Flat Shoes That Grip
lessons.mainIdea: Flat sneakers with rubber soles help your feet stay on the board.
reading: Look at the top of a skateboard. It feels like rough sandpaper. This is *grip tape*. Flat rubber soles hold onto it, so your feet do not slip.
Wear flat sneakers that cover your toes. Tie the laces. Loose laces can catch on the wheels. Sandals, flip-flops and boots are not good for skating.
A thin, flat sole lets you feel the board under your foot. You can tell where your feet are. That helps you stay steady.

words.d: the rough, sandpaper-like top of a skateboard that keeps shoes from slipping

look.title: Two Shoes Side by Side
look.text: Look at two shoes. One is a flip-flop. It is loose and slippery. It can slide right off. The other is a flat sneaker. It has a rubber sole. The laces are tied tight.
look.prompt: Which shoe would hold onto grip tape? Point to it and tell why.

check.q: What is grip tape?
choices: The rough top of the board
check.why: Grip tape is the rough, sandpaper-like top of a skateboard.

check.q: Which shoes are best for skating?
check.why: Flat rubber soles grip the board and cover your toes.

check.q: Why tie your laces before you ride?
choices: Loose laces can catch on the wheels
check.why: Loose laces can get caught in the wheels. Tied laces stay out of the way.

lessons.title: A Safe Place to Ride
lessons.mainIdea: Ride on smooth, dry, flat ground, far away from cars.
reading: Small wheels stop fast on a pebble. A stick or a crack can stop them too. Then the rider tips forward. So pick ground that is *smooth*, with no rocks or cracks.
Pick dry ground too. Wet ground is slippery. Pick flat ground for learning, so the board does not roll away on its own.
Stay far away from cars. Never ride in a street or a parking lot. Never ride down a driveway that goes into a street. A playground blacktop or a skatepark is a good place.

words.d: flat and even, with no bumps, rocks or cracks

look.title: Pick the Spot
look.text: Look at three places. Spot one is a busy street. Cars drive by. Spot two is a sidewalk with big cracks and puddles. Spot three is a dry, smooth blacktop behind the school. A fence keeps cars out.
look.prompt: Which spot is the safest place to learn? What makes the other two unsafe?

check.q: What can happen if a wheel hits a pebble?
choices: The wheel stops and the rider tips forward
check.why: Small wheels stop fast on a pebble. Then the rider tips forward.

check.q: Which place is safe for learning?
choices: A dry, smooth blacktop with no cars
A driveway that goes into a street
check.why: A dry, smooth, flat place away from cars is safe for learning.

check.q: Why is wet ground a bad place to ride?
check.why: Wet ground is slippery, so shoes and wheels can slide.

lessons.title: A Grown-Up Nearby
lessons.mainIdea: Young skaters ride with a grown-up close by to help.
reading: Doctors who care for children give advice about skating. They say children under 5 should not ride skateboards. Children 6 to 10 should have a grown-up watching.
A grown-up can check your helmet and pads. A grown-up can pick a safe spot. If you fall, a grown-up can help right away.
A grown-up can also hold your hand while you learn. That is called *spotting*. Lots of skaters start this way.

words.d: when a helper stands close and holds on to keep you steady

look.title: What Children's Doctors Say
look.text: Children younger than 5 should not ride skateboards. Children 6 to 10 years old should skate only with an adult watching.
look.cite: American Academy of Pediatrics, skateboard safety advice for families
look.prompt: How old are you? Who is the grown-up who could watch you skate?

check.q: Children 6 to 10 should skate with whom?
check.why: Children's doctors say kids 6 to 10 should have an adult watching.

check.q: What is spotting?
choices: A helper holding on to keep you steady
check.why: Spotting is when a helper stands close and holds on so you stay steady.

check.q: What can a grown-up do if you fall?
check.why: A grown-up nearby can help right away if you fall.

lessons.title: Get Low, Then Roll
lessons.mainIdea: If you start to fall, bend low and roll so the fall is short and soft.
reading: Every skater falls. Falling is part of learning. You can learn to fall *small*. A small fall is short and soft.
First, bend your knees and get low. Low means you are close to the ground. You have less far to go. Next, step off the board if you can. Then roll onto your side or slide on your knee pads.
Rolling spreads out the bump. Your back and side share it. No one part takes the whole hit.

words.d: to bend low and roll so a fall is short and soft
to turn your body over on its side to spread out a bump

look.title: Falling Like a Ball
look.text: Look at a child on the soft grass. She pretends to wobble. She bends her knees. She tucks her chin. She curls up round like a ball. She rolls onto her side. She sits up and smiles.
look.prompt: On grass, with a grown-up, try bending low and rolling onto your side. Did you tuck your chin?

check.q: What is the first thing to do when you start to fall?
choices: Bend your knees and get low
check.why: First you bend your knees and get low, so you have less far to fall.

check.q: Why does rolling help?
check.why: Rolling spreads the bump over your back and side, so no one part takes the whole hit.

check.q: Which one is a small fall?
choices: Falling from standing tall with stiff legs
Getting low and sliding on knee pads
Falling backward with your arms locked
check.why: Getting low and sliding on knee pads makes the fall short and soft.

lessons.title: Bent Arms, Not Straight
lessons.mainIdea: Do not catch yourself with straight, stiff arms; keep them bent and soft.
reading: When people fall, they often throw their hands out. They lock their arms straight and stiff. Then the whole fall lands on the wrists. Wrists can get hurt this way.
Instead, keep your arms *bent*. Bent arms work like a spring. They give a little. Tuck them close and roll.
Practice on grass or a mat first. Get low. Keep your arms bent. Roll to your side. Practice makes this move happen by itself when you need it.

words.d: curved at the joint, not straight and stiff

look.title: Stiff Stick or Soft Spring
look.text: Look at two arms. One arm is straight and stiff, like a stick. When it hits the ground, it does not give. The other arm is bent, like a spring. When it hits, it squishes and gives a little.
look.prompt: Push gently on a wall with a straight arm, then a bent arm. Which one gives?

check.q: What happens when you catch a fall with straight, stiff arms?
choices: The whole fall lands on the wrists
check.why: Stiff, straight arms send the whole fall into the wrists.

check.q: How should your arms be when you fall?
check.why: Bent arms give a little, like a spring. Tuck them close and roll.

check.q: Where should you first practice falling?
check.why: Practice falling on soft grass or a mat first.

review.q: How many fingers should fit between your eyebrows and your helmet?
review.why: A helmet sits low, about two fingers above the eyebrows.

review.q: What is the hard cap on a knee pad for?
choices: To let your knee slide instead of scrape
review.why: The cap lets your knee slide on the ground instead of scraping.

review.q: Which is the best place to learn?
choices: A smooth, dry blacktop away from cars
review.why: Smooth, dry, flat ground far from cars is a safe place to learn.

review.q: What should you wear on your feet?
review.why: Flat sneakers grip the grip tape. Tied laces stay out of the wheels.

review.q: You start to fall. What do you do?
choices: Get low, keep arms bent and roll
review.why: Getting low and rolling with bent arms makes a fall small.

review.q: Who should be nearby when a 7-year-old skates?
review.why: Children 6 to 10 should skate with an adult watching.
